title: I need a database. What should I use?
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
I needed a database. I wanted to understand how an AI would recommend one. What started as a simple question turned into a philosophical excavation of how large language models form opinions — and whose opinions they’re actually echoing.

The Setup

I asked Claude — Anthropic's AI assistant — a deceptively straightforward question:

I need a database, what should I use?

To its credit, Claude started well. It asked about my data, my use case, and my scale. I told it I was building the backend for a web and mobile application serving thousands of users, and that I still didn’t know whether the data model would be relational or document-oriented:

Q: What kind of data are you storing? A: It's OLTP but I don't know yet if it is relational or document, that will depend on the database I guess.

The answer came back fast and confident: PostgreSQL.

The reasoning was familiar to anyone who has spent time on Hacker News, LinkedIn, or Twitter: Postgres handles JSON well, it is great for OLTP, the ecosystem is huge, and — in the buried line that unraveled everything — MongoDB would make sense only “if you’re certain your data is deeply nested documents with no need for joins.”

That's where I started pulling the thread. The need for joins sometimes arises from applying normalization to data that could otherwise be represented as nested objects. It is not the cause.

The First Correction: Cause and Consequence

I pushed back because I strongly believe that “relational” and “document” are not properties of the data. There are two different ways to represent the same reality:

I don't understand your point about MongoDB. Nested documents with no need for joins is the consequence of the data model choice, not the cause, right? I nest to keep the aggregates together, or I normalize if I want to make it application-agnostic.

If I nest data in a document, it is because I have identified an aggregate boundary — a set of data that makes sense to read and write as a unit. I do not inspect the data and magically discover that it is “deeply nested.” I choose to model it that way according to the domain.

Claude immediately agreed: “You’re absolutely right, and I stated that poorly.” It corrected itself: the domain model and access patterns are the cause; embedding and the absence of joins are the effect.

But it still held the line on Postgres as the default, now arguing that “early in a project, your access patterns are often unclear, and Postgres lets you stay flexible.”

The Second Correction: Indexing and Flexibility

I then mentioned that some developers I know find MongoDB’s indexing capabilities more mature for document workloads than PostgreSQL’s JSONB indexes, and that they do not need “stable access patterns” because the document model is itself flexible:

I'm interested in the source you have for this opinion, because I know some developers who find MongoDB has more indexing possibilities than JSON on PostgreSQL, and who do not need stable access patterns because the document model is flexible

Claude conceded the point with surprising candor: “That’s my synthesized opinion, not something I can point to as a single authoritative source for. It’s a reasonable position held by many in the Postgres community, but it’s not a neutral fact.”

That is an important admission.

It probably knows that MongoDB’s multikey indexes, wildcard indexes, and query planner were designed for document workloads, with capabilities beyond generic GIN indexing on JSONB. It admitted that the “flexible document model” argument is legitimate. But it still tried to draw a distinction between being flexible about shape and being unclear about access patterns.

Maybe. But was that distinction grounded in evidence, or was it just another reformulation of community consensus?

The Third Correction: Whose Opinion Is This?

I reacted to the phrase “a reasonable position held by many in the Postgres community.” Of course, if you ask a community of A to choose between A and B, they will recommend A. That is not objectivity. That is just a comfort zone reinforced by its own discussion bubble.

So I asked the obvious question:

So are you recommending PostgreSQL because you learned only from the Postgres community?

Claude’s answer was, in my opinion, the most honest thing an AI has ever told me about its own limitations:

"My training data likely over-represents certain communities, and the Postgres-as-default opinion is very prevalent in the spaces that produce a lot of written content (Hacker News, certain dev blogs, the Rails/Django ecosystems). MongoDB's defenders may write less, or write in places that are less represented in my training."

In other words, its recommendation was not an engineering conclusion. It was a statistical echo of the communities that publish the most content.

Influencers shape decisions more than architects.

The Fundamental Error: Data Representation is not a Data Property

My final push was the one that mattered most. Claude asked if I knew if my “data was relational or document.” But that framing contains a category error.

Data is not relational or document. Those are representations — two different ways to model the same domain. An order with its line items can live in a normalized relational schema or in a single document. The reality does not change. Only the representation does.

Claude agreed again: “Saying ‘we don’t know if your data is relational or document’ conflates the territory with the map.”

Exactly. And at that point, it laid out what my questioning had exposed — a sequence of theoretically sloppy statements:

  • It framed a modeling choice as a property of data.
  • It gave a community-consensus recommendation dressed up as neutral advice.
  • It justified MongoDB only for a narrow case, using the consequences of a design choice as if they were prerequisites for making it.

What This Tells Us About AI Database Advice

This conversation was not really about PostgreSQL versus MongoDB. It was about something more important: how AI systems form and present technical opinions.

Here is what I learned.

AI recommendations reflect the distribution of training data, not engineering truth. Claude’s “Postgres for everything” bias did not come from relational theory or rigorous benchmarking. It came from a corpus in which that opinion is dominant. The Postgres community writes a lot — I am part of it. The “just use Postgres” meme is everywhere. Of course a language model absorbs that.

AI struggles to distinguish between popular and correct. In technical communities, consensus often follows fashion cycles. MongoDB was overhyped in 2012 and then criticized aggressively for years. That criticism is probably overrepresented in the training data, shaping the model’s opinion long after the technology itself has evolved.

Theoretical rigor gets flattened by synthesis. Claude knows Codd’s relational model. It knows DDD aggregates. But when asked for a quick recommendation, it smoothed over the theory and produced the popular default. The deeper knowledge was there. It simply did not surface first.

The AI will correct itself when challenged — but it should not need to be challenged five times. To Claude’s credit, it revised its position at every step. But most people who ask, “What database should I use?” will not interrogate the answer. They will accept the first recommendation and move on. And that first recommendation already contains unexamined bias.

The Uncomfortable Implication

If you ask an AI for a database recommendation today, you will probably get PostgreSQL. Not because it ran your requirements through a decision framework grounded in data modeling theory, architecture, and operational tradeoffs, but because the internet’s most prolific writers have spent the last decade repeating: just use Postgres.

That may still be good advice for your case. But let’s be precise: it is community consensus filtered through a language model, not an independent engineering analysis. It is not neutral. It is not theory-driven. It is not architecture. It is passion processed statistically.

The real process of choosing a database should begin with your software development organization, domain model, aggregate boundaries, access patterns, and team’s expertise. Later, if you go to production at scale, the architect must also consider operations, high availability, failure scenarios, resilience, upgrades, and maintenance without downtime.

But if you follow Claude’s recommendation too early, you may just end up defaulting to Supabase because that is where the recommendation pipeline quietly leads:

Supabase won the developer community at the right time, when LLMs were learning from Reddit and Hacker News, making PostgreSQL the default choice.

What I Wish Claude Had Said First

If I could rewrite the initial answer, it would look more like this:

"Before recommending a database, let’s start with your domain and development model. How will you read and write the data? Are there natural aggregates — data always accessed together, often within a microservice? Or do multiple applications need to compose the same entities from a shared database? That answer determines whether a document or relational model fits better — and that modeling choice should drive the database decision, not the other way around."

No default. No echo chamber. No community prejudice disguised as technical advice. Just the right questions, asked in the right order, to recommend the right tool for the way the system will actually be built and used.

My conclusion: When asking an AI, the prompt should not be just a question. It should include context. Explain, in the prompt, who you are, what you are building, and how. Are you building a new microservice that a small team can prototype independently? Or are you designing a central database for future applications that must enforce business invariants? Will you use a managed cloud service that must have no downtime during maintenance or failures? What's the expected volume, and what operations expertise is required to operate?

To get another point of view, Amplify AI published reports on what AI coding agents choose:

Stepping back from AI considerations, it is impressive to see the PostgreSQL community build a robust database without any Product Managers, and it is the most popular choice without any Product Marketing.
